## Topics covered

-   The sampling distribution of a statistic
-   Standard error
-   The central limit theorem
-   Bias and mean squared error of an estimator

::: callout-note
#### Note

The exercises associated with this unit are available at
[this link](https://tommasorigon.github.io/EnvEcoStat/exe/exe_C.html).
:::

## A survey on climate change

In 2019, a poll asked a [random sample]{.blue} of $n = 1008$ Americans whether
they thought that climate change was a major threat to the stability of the
United States. A total of $524$ people said yes.

```{r}
524 / 1008 # Sample proportion
```

The [sample proportion]{.orange} $\hat{\pi} = 0.52$ is a [statistic]{.blue}. The
population proportion $\pi$ is a [parameter]{.orange}: it is unknown, because we
cannot interview all the Americans.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Can we conclude that the [majority]{.orange} of Americans thinks that climate
change is a major threat?
:::

## What if exactly half said yes?

Suppose that $\pi = 0.5$. Then the number of yes in a sample of $1008$ people is
a $\text{binom}(1008, 0.5)$. With `rbinom` ([Unit H](un_H.html)) we can simulate $R = 5000$
[new surveys]{.blue}:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
R <- 5000 # Number of simulated surveys
pi_hat <- rbinom(R, size = 1008, prob = 0.5) / 1008 # R sample proportions
head(pi_hat)
```

Each survey gives a different value: before collecting the data, $\hat{\pi}$ is
a [random variable]{.orange}. Its distribution is called [sampling
distribution]{.blue}.

```{r}
hist(pi_hat, breaks = 30, main = "Sample proportions (n = 1008)", xlab = "Sample proportion")
abline(v = 0.52, col = "red") # Observed sample proportion
```

How often does a survey give $52\%$ of yes or more, if $\pi = 0.5$?

```{r}
mean(pi_hat >= 0.52) # The mean of TRUE / FALSE values is a proportion
```

About $1$ survey out of $10$: the observed result is [not surprising]{.orange},
and we cannot conclude that there is a majority.

## Standard error

The theory says that $$
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\pi}] = \pi, \qquad \sigma_{\hat{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}.
$$

The quantity $\sigma_{\hat{\pi}}$ is the [standard error]{.orange}: it measures
how much $\hat{\pi}$ varies from sample to sample.

```{r}
mean(pi_hat) # Simulated
sd(pi_hat) # Simulated
sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / 1008) # Theoretical standard error
```

The standard error [decreases]{.blue} with $n$. With $n = 10000$ people, the
same $52\%$ would have been very surprising:

```{r}
sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / 10000)
```

{{< video video/un_I_survey.mp4 title="The sampling distribution of the sample proportion" >}}

## Air pollution in a city

An environmental agency wants to estimate the mean daily concentration $\mu$ of
PM2.5 (in µg/m³) in a city, measuring it on $n = 64$ random days.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

[Before]{.orange} collecting the data: how close to $\mu$ will the sample mean
$\bar{y}$ of $64$ days be?
:::

From previous years, the daily concentrations have mean about $28$, standard
deviation about $12$, and an [asymmetric]{.blue} distribution. We describe them
with a [gamma]{.orange} distribution with these mean and standard deviation:

```{r}
mu <- 28
sigma <- 12
k <- mu^2 / sigma^2 # Shape, so that the mean is mu
lambda <- mu / sigma^2 # Rate, so that the standard deviation is sigma
curve(dgamma(x, shape = k, rate = lambda), from = 0, to = 100, xlab = "PM2.5", ylab = "f(y)")
```

## Repeating the experiment

A simulated campaign of $64$ days, repeated three times:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 64
mean(rgamma(n, shape = k, rate = lambda))
mean(rgamma(n, shape = k, rate = lambda))
mean(rgamma(n, shape = k, rate = lambda))
```

We want $R = 5000$ campaigns, so we use a `for` loop ([Unit B](un_B.html)):

```{r}
y_bar <- rep(NA, R) # Empty vector, to be filled with the R sample means

for (r in 1:R) {
  y <- rgamma(n, shape = k, rate = lambda) # A new campaign of n days
  y_bar[r] <- mean(y) # Its sample mean is stored in position r
}
```

::: callout-tip
#### Hint

If the loop is not clear, set `R <- 3` and run it again, adding `print(y_bar)`
inside the curly brackets.
:::

## The sampling distribution of $\bar{Y}$

The theory says that $$
\mathbb{E}[\bar{Y}] = \mu, \qquad \sigma_{\bar{Y}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

```{r}
mean(y_bar) # Simulated
sd(y_bar) # Simulated
sigma / sqrt(n) # Theoretical standard error
```

The [central limit theorem]{.orange} states that, for large $n$, $$
\bar{Y} \simeq \text{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$ regardless of the shape of the population. Indeed:

```{r}
hist(y_bar, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, main = "Sample means (n = 64)", xlab = "Sample mean")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma / sqrt(n)), add = TRUE, col = "red")
```

The option `add = TRUE` draws the curve on top of the histogram.

## Using the central limit theorem

What is the probability that the campaign [overestimates]{.orange} $\mu$ by more
than $3$ µg/m³, that is $\mathbb{P}(\bar{Y} > 31)$? We can answer either with the
central limit theorem or with the simulated sample means:

```{r}
1 - pnorm(31, mean = mu, sd = sigma / sqrt(n)) # Central limit theorem
mean(y_bar > 31) # Simulation
```

{{< video video/un_I_pm25.mp4 title="Repeated campaigns and the central limit theorem" >}}

## Estimating the variance

In [Unit E](un_E.html) and [Unit F](un_F.html) we saw that `var` divides by
$n - 1$ and not by $n$. Why? Consider the two estimators of $\sigma^2$ $$
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2, \qquad S^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2.
$$

An estimator is [unbiased]{.blue} if its expected value equals the parameter.
Let us check through simulation, with a short campaign of $n = 5$ days:

```{r}
my_var <- function(x) mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 # From Unit F: divides by n

set.seed(123)
n <- 5
R <- 10000
sigma2_hat <- rep(NA, R)
S2 <- rep(NA, R)

for (r in 1:R) {
  y <- rgamma(n, shape = k, rate = lambda)
  sigma2_hat[r] <- my_var(y)
  S2[r] <- var(y)
}

c(mean(sigma2_hat), mean(S2), sigma^2)
```

$S^2$ is [unbiased]{.orange}, whereas $\hat{\sigma}^2$ underestimates $\sigma^2$,
since $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}^2] = (n-1)\sigma^2 / n = 115.2$.

## Mean squared error

Unbiasedness is not everything. The [mean squared error]{.blue} $$
\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{\theta} - \mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}])^2] + (\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta)^2
$$ measures how close, on average, an estimator falls to the parameter:

```{r}
mean((sigma2_hat - sigma^2)^2) # MSE of the biased estimator
mean((S2 - sigma^2)^2) # MSE of the unbiased estimator
```

The biased estimator has a [smaller]{.orange} MSE: its bias is compensated by a
smaller variance (the bias-variance trade-off).
